title: Detection Strategy for Hidden Virtual Instance Execution
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Hidden Virtual Instance Execution
summary: This strategy detects a hidden virtual instance, the technique recorded in the assignment as t1564-006, where malicious code runs inside a virtual machine or container that the user is not meant to see. The hidden instance gives the attacker an isolated place to unpack payloads, stage tooling or evade analysis, while the host only shows a virtualization process starting. Useful telemetry includes process creation with parent and command line, hypervisor or container service logs, virtual machine configuration files written to user profiles, and image load events from the guest runtime libraries. Detection fails when it matches virtualization tooling alone, because legitimate administrators and developers start virtual machines constantly; the target directory, the naming of the instance and the absence of any management path are what raise confidence.

beginner.definition: A virtual machine is a computer that runs inside another computer as a program. A hidden virtual instance is one the user never sees, created quietly by malware. The attacker works inside it so their tools stay away from the normal desktop.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools often watch the normal operating system closely. A hidden guest can look like clean traffic leaving one program. It also gives the attacker a safe place to store tools between steps. Because the guest is disposable, cleaning the host may not remove everything. Detecting the hidden instance removes both the workspace and the hiding place.
howItWorks: A program on the host starts a virtualisation service or a hypervisor process.
It creates a guest configuration, usually a group of files in a folder on the disk.
The guest starts and runs code that the host operating system cannot easily inspect.
The endpoint agent records process creation, file creation and library loading on the host.
The rule matches virtualisation processes that are started by unexpected parents or that write configuration into user folders.
It then checks whether the instance has no connection to your approved management tools, and alerts if it does not.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where a supervisor checks every trolley at the gate. Someone builds a sealed room in a corner of the warehouse and works inside it. The gate stays quiet because nothing passes it. The clue is the construction work and the new door, not any trolley.
takeaways: A hidden guest hides activity from host level monitoring.
Virtualisation processes and guest configuration files are the visible traces.
Approved management tooling is the baseline that separates legitimate virtual machines from hidden ones.

objectives: Explain why running code inside a hidden virtual instance helps an attacker
Identify the host events that appear when a virtual machine or container starts
Describe how guest configuration and disk files reveal a hidden instance
Distinguish managed virtualisation platforms from unmanaged local virtual machines
Write a rule that scores parent process, target directory and instance naming
Explain the limits of host based inspection for activity inside a guest
dataSources: Sysmon event 1 process creation capturing virtualisation executables, their parent image and command line
Sysmon event 11 file creation for virtual machine configuration and disk files written outside approved virtualisation storage
Sysmon event 7 image load showing guest runtime or hypervisor libraries loaded into an unexpected host process
Windows hypervisor platform or container service operational logs recording instance creation and start events
Virtualisation management inventory listing hosts, clusters and storage locations approved for running guests
logic: The rule focuses on the host side evidence that a guest started without the management plane knowing. It selects process creation for hypervisor and container runtime binaries, then filters out instances started by the approved management agents or by service accounts that own the virtualisation platform, and it adds file creation events where guest configuration or disk files appear in user profile, temporary or download directories. Ransomware and loaders that use this technique typically create anonymous or randomly named instances with no registered management record, so the strongest alert is a guest runtime start that writes configuration outside approved storage and never appears in the virtualisation inventory. Correlating the process parent with the file path is what separates a developer's local virtual machine from a hidden instance.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unmanaged Virtual Instance Started on Host
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: sysmon
# detection:
#   selection_proc:
#     EventID: 1
#     Image|endswith:
#       - vmware-vmx.exe
#       - VBoxHeadless.exe
#       - qemu-system-x86_64.exe
#   selection_file:
#     EventID: 11
#     TargetFilename|contains: \Users\
#     TargetFilename|endswith:
#       - .vmdk
#       - .vhdx
#       - .qcow2
#   filter_managed:
#     ParentImage|endswith: \vdi-broker.exe
#   condition: (selection_proc or selection_file) and not filter_managed
# level: high
falsePositives: Developers who run local virtual machines for testing and store them under their own user profile directory
Security analysts who build isolated laboratory guests on their workstations outside the central virtualisation platform
Training sessions where participants create temporary virtual machines from a downloaded appliance image
Vendor support engineers who reproduce a customer issue in a local guest during a remote session
Container development tools that start lightweight virtual machines for building images on developer laptops
tuningNotes: Scope the rule to hosts that are not part of the approved virtualisation estate, using your hypervisor inventory as an exclusion list rather than excluding all virtualisation processes, and keep server coverage where guests should never start outside the platform. Allowlist the exact parent processes and service accounts that manage approved guests, and alert separately on any guest runtime start whose configuration files land in a user profile or temporary directory. The coverage you lose by excluding managed platforms is the case of an attacker who compromises the management plane itself, so pair this rule with privileged account monitoring on the virtualisation administrators and with alerts on new hosts joining the cluster.
